articles.heading: Purpose and Format of the FIDE Arbiter Exam
articles.content:
Chapter 12 contains sample examination questions of the type used in FIDE Arbiter seminars. These questions are drawn from all major areas of the Arbiters' Manual.

Exam format:
- The FIDE Arbiter seminar exam consists of multiple-choice questions
- Each question typically has four options (A, B, C, D)
- A score of at least 80% is required to pass
- The exam is conducted under supervision at the end of the seminar
- Time allowed is typically 90 minutes to 2 hours
- Mobile phones and reference materials are not permitted during the exam

Topics covered:
1. Laws of Chess (Articles 1–12, Appendices A–D, Guidelines)
2. Swiss pairing systems (Dutch System, Baku Acceleration)
3. Round robin scheduling (Berger table)
4. Rating regulations (Elo formula, K-factors, reporting)
5. Title regulations (GM, IM, FM, FA, IA requirements)
6. Anti-cheating regulations and procedures
7. Technical recommendations (equipment standards)
8. Competition regulations (tiebreaks, appeals, withdrawals)
9. Online chess regulations
10. Practical arbitering scenarios

Candidates are advised to study the full Arbiters' Manual and to attend at least one live tournament as an observer or assistant arbiter before sitting the exam.

articles.heading: Sample Questions — Laws of Chess
articles.content:
Sample exam questions on the Laws of Chess:

Q1: A player makes a move and before pressing the clock, realises it is illegal. What should happen?
A) The move stands as it has been released
B) The player may correct the move since the clock has not yet been pressed
C) The game is lost immediately
D) The arbiter must intervene
Answer: B — An illegal move is only completed when the clock is pressed (Article 7.5.1). Until the clock is pressed, the player may correct their move.

Q2: During time trouble, a player picks up their king and a rook at the same time intending to castle. What is the correct ruling?
A) The player must move the king only
B) The player must castle on that side if legal (Article 4.4.1)
C) The player may make any legal move
D) The game is lost
Answer: B — Touching the king and rook simultaneously obliges the player to castle on that side if legal.

Q3: A player offers a draw BEFORE making their move. What should the arbiter do?
A) Declare the draw offer invalid
B) Accept the draw offer on behalf of both players
C) The draw offer is valid but made at the wrong time; apply Article 12.9
D) Require the game to continue
Answer: C — A draw offer made at the wrong time (before the move) is still valid per Article 9.1.2.1, but the deviation from correct procedure should be penalised per Article 12.9.

articles.heading: Sample Questions — Swiss Pairings and Tournament Systems
articles.content:
Sample exam questions on tournament systems:

Q1: In the Dutch Swiss system, how is the top half of a score bracket paired against the bottom half?
A) Randomly
B) S1 vs S(n/2+1), S2 vs S(n/2+2), etc.
C) By drawing of lots within each group
D) The highest-ranked player meets the lowest-ranked player
Answer: B — The Dutch System pairs the top half against the bottom half in order within each score bracket.

Q2: A player withdraws from a 9-round Swiss tournament after completing 4 games. What happens to the results of the 4 games played?
A) All 4 games stand and are counted for both the withdrawn player and their opponents
B) All 4 games are cancelled since 4 is less than 50% of 9
C) Only the first 2 games stand
D) The arbiter decides case by case
Answer: B — 4 games is less than 50% of 9 (4.5 required). Per Article C05.3, results are cancelled if fewer than 50% of games are completed.

Q3: In the Baku Acceleration system, what are the virtual points used for?
A) They count toward the final tournament score
B) Pairing purposes only — they do not affect the real tournament score
C) Determining colour allocation only
D) Seeding for the second half of the tournament
Answer: B — Virtual points in the Baku Acceleration are used only for pairing purposes and are removed once the acceleration rounds are completed.

articles.heading: Sample Questions — Rating and Title Regulations
articles.content:
Sample exam questions on ratings and titles:

Q1: What is the K-factor for a player who has achieved a published rating of 2400 in the past but is currently rated 2350?
A) K = 40
B) K = 20
C) K = 10
D) K = 30
Answer: C — Per B02.8, the K-factor is 10 for any player who has EVER had a published standard rating of 2400 or above, regardless of their current rating.

Q2: A player achieves a performance rating of 2610 in a 9-round norm event with the required proportion of titled opponents and federation diversity. What title norm have they achieved?
A) FM norm (Rp ≥ 2300)
B) IM norm (Rp ≥ 2450)
C) GM norm (Rp ≥ 2600)
D) No norm — minimum 10 games are required
Answer: C — A GM norm requires Rp ≥ 2600 and a minimum of 9 games. Both conditions are met.

Q3: An arbiter fails the FIDE Arbiter seminar examination with a score of 74%. What can the arbiter do?
A) Appeal the result to ARB
B) Retake the exam at the next available seminar (the 80% threshold was not met)
C) Apply for the FA title anyway since 74% is close to the threshold
D) The result is final and the arbiter cannot retake the exam
Answer: B — Candidates who fail (score below 80%) may retake the exam at the next available seminar.

articles.heading: Sample Questions — Practical Arbitering Scenarios
articles.content:
Sample practical scenario questions:

Q1: During a game, a player's mobile phone rings in the playing venue. The game is not yet decisive (the player has a winning position). What must the arbiter do?
A) Give the player a warning and continue
B) Declare the game lost for the player with the phone — the opponent wins (Article 11.3.2.2)
C) Add 2 minutes to the opponent's clock
D) Pause the game and hold the phone in escrow until the game ends
Answer: B — Per Article 11.3.2.2, if it is evident a player has an electronic device in the playing venue, they shall lose the game and the opponent shall win, regardless of the position.

Q2: An arbiter notices that the colours at Board 5 have been reversed compared to the pairings. 7 moves have been played. What should the arbiter do?
A) Cancel the game immediately and start again
B) Stop the game and restart with correct colours since fewer than 10 moves have been made by both players (Article 7.3)
C) Allow the game to continue since moves have already been made
D) Ask the players to agree on what to do
Answer: B — Per Article 7.3, if a game has started with colours reversed and fewer than 10 moves have been made by both players, it shall be discontinued and a new game played.

Q3: Both players have less than 2 minutes remaining and neither is recording moves. The arbiter cannot determine how many moves have been made. A player claims a win on time. What should the arbiter do?
A) Immediately declare a win for the claimant
B) Declare a draw since neither player can prove the time control was reached
C) Pause the clock, reconstruct the game from both scoresheets and use the move counter if available; declare the result based on the information obtained (Articles 8.5, 6.4)
D) Add 10 minutes to both clocks and continue
Answer: C — The arbiter should reconstruct the game using all available information per Articles 8.5 and 6.4, then apply the correct result.

articles.heading: Sample Questions — Anti-Cheating and Online Regulations
articles.content:
Sample questions on anti-cheating and online chess:

Q1: What is the Z-score threshold for presumption of cheating in over-the-board chess under the FIDE Anti-Cheating Regulations?
A) Z > 2.50
B) Z > 3.00
C) Z > 4.25
D) Z > 5.00
Answer: D — Per Article 1.6 of the Anti-Cheating Regulations, the threshold for OTB chess is 5.00. (Online chess uses 4.25.)

Q2: A player in a supervised online competition disconnects for 4 minutes during a critical stage of the game. The tournament regulations specify a disconnection threshold of 3 minutes. What may the arbiter do?
A) Nothing — disconnections are always technical errors and cannot be penalised
B) Declare the game lost for the disconnected player, since the threshold has been exceeded
C) Add 5 minutes to the disconnected player's clock
D) Pause both clocks and wait indefinitely for reconnection
Answer: B — Per Article E04.11, if the disconnection exceeds the specified threshold, the arbiter may declare the game lost for the disconnected player.

Q3: Which of the following is defined as 'sandbagging' under FIDE's Anti-Cheating Regulations?
A) Using a computer to find the best move during a game
B) Deliberately playing below one's ability to lower one's rating for future events
C) Refusing to be searched by the Fair Play Officer
D) Playing under a false identity
Answer: B — Sandbagging is specifically defined in Article 1.2b as deliberately playing below one's actual ability in order to lower one's rating to play in future events with a better chance of winning.
